Understand Profitability by Product and Sales Channel

Thematic Area: Food Cost Intelligence & Commercial Decision Support

How might we calculate reliable product and channel contribution margins to guide pricing, sourcing and operating decisions?

Background

An Indonesian healthy-food retailer sells raw ingredients, grocery products and prepared foods through different channels. The opportunity is to make product and channel economics clear and actionable.

The objective is to connect revenue with ingredient, purchasing, yield, handling, processing, packaging, delivery, fee and promotion costs. Consistent contribution-margin calculations support pricing, sourcing and operating decisions.

Relevant startups offer product-cost modelling, finance-data integration and scenario analysis. The collaboration centres on a shared costing method and records that connect commercial decisions with their financial effect.

Significance of Problem

The key challenges are:

  • Less informed pricing: Missing costs produce an incomplete view of the economics behind prices and promotions.
  • Unclear channel trade-offs: Delivery charges, commissions and discounts affect the contribution generated by each sales channel.
  • Inconsistent benefit measurement: Yield, allocated costs and shared benefits need consistent treatment to compare product and channel decisions.

Existing Efforts

  • Available modelling capability: A cost-management platform organises cost inputs, assumptions, scenario comparisons and approvals. Recipes, saleable output, packaging and channel costs form the basis of a food-product model.
  • First application: Select one prepared-food product and one channel. Define the costing method and reconcile the model with purchasing, production and finance records. Compare pricing, ingredient or packaging scenarios using transparent assumptions.
  • Collaboration focus: Set data ownership and update frequency, with a consistent treatment of wastage, returns and shared costs. Use the model to support a selected commercial decision and track its realised margin effect.

Potential Market Size

  • Indonesian grocery-retail scale: Indonesia’s grocery retail sales reached approximately US$106.2 billion in 2025. This provides a substantial customer-industry base for product-cost intelligence and commercial decision support.

Eligibility / Qualification

  • Technology readiness: Minimum technology readiness level 3 (TRL3).
  • NUS linkage: NUS student or graduate founder, or incubation through an NUS programme such as BLOCK71.
  • Local and overseas startups: Open to Indonesian and overseas startups.
  • Commitment: Complete the selection process and travel to Indonesia if selected.
